name: Zaleplon

lead: Zaleplon (Sonata) is a prescription sleep medicine for short-term insomnia, notable for a half-life of about one hour. People in recovery circles connect easier sleep onset with less puffiness, clearer skin and a more rested face.

It binds the BZ1 site on the GABA-A receptor, enhancing inhibitory signalling to induce sleep. Its short half-life is reported to reduce next-day effects. It has been studied for insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

paras: It is used on prescription for trouble falling asleep, taken at bedtime for short periods. People pair it with regular sleep timing, with any looks benefit expected to come from accumulated better nights.
Reported effects include headache, dizziness, sleepiness, amnesia and complex sleep behaviors; dependence can occur with prolonged use. It is Schedule IV in the US and prescription-only.

angle.text: Zaleplon (Sonata) is a short-acting prescription Z-drug for falling asleep. The idea is quicker sleep onset, better overnight recovery, then clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It has been studied for insomnia.

lead: Zaleplon, sold as Sonata, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic (pyrazolopyrimidine class) approved for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly difficulty falling asleep.[1]

It acts at the BZ1 site of the GABA-A receptor and has a very short half-life of about one hour, which Grokipedia says reduces next-day effects.[1] It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[1]
It has no approved or studied appearance use. Its inclusion in this wiki reflects its place among sleep medicines discussed in recovery contexts.

paras: Zaleplon is indicated for short-term insomnia treatment taken immediately before bed when several hours of sleep are possible.[1][2] Its short half-life is described as suiting people who need to wake early.[1]

Common effects include headache, dizziness and somnolence; serious risks include complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving, anterograde amnesia, and dependence with prolonged use.[1][2] Dose reduction is advised for older people and those with hepatic impairment.[1]

A BMJ meta-analysis examined benefits and risks of short-term sedative hypnotics, including zaleplon, in older people with insomnia, covering sleep measures, adverse events and morning-after psychomotor impairment.[3] An earlier meta-analysis compared pharmacotherapy with behavioural therapy for persistent insomnia.[4] The AASM guideline and a Lancet network meta-analysis assess hypnotics for chronic insomnia.[5][6] A cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality, though observational designs cannot show causation.[7] Pharmacological reviews describe the drug class.[8]
No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
